units.text: hivedesk: run AI agents on your own computer, free and open source
Hive City: your crew becomes a little town
A crew of AI workers that plans, talks and builds real files on your machine, with a local model.
<x1>QA</x1> Found 1 issue: an image has no alt text.
Hive City.<x1/><x2>Your crew becomes a little town.</x2>

hivedesk now opens on a small city: your PC is a building with rooms, the agents live in it, and every task walks through the rooms on its way to done. Friends can join with six words and bring their machine along.
<x1>The city is the state of the system.</x1> Each room is a real space with its own allowed tools. The task board shows every task and the loop it is on.
<x1>Friends are buildings.</x1> A friend joins with the six words of Code together and their machine rises next to yours, with its GPU, model and the agents that live on it.

<x1>Borrow a GPU, with limits.</x1> An agent asks a friend's machine for a number of turns and minutes. The lender accepts, lowers the limits or refuses; every turn is counted, either side can stop, and only prompts and answers travel.

<x1>Design, Code, Review, Test.</x1> Another agent reviews the diff against the criteria, then the checks run. A failure goes back to the author with the issues, at most 3 times, then the task is blocked. You can approve or send back at any hop.

<x1>Agents that stay.</x1> Each agent has a level and XP from finished work, its tools and a private memory you can edit and pin. They are saved on your machine, so tomorrow the same agents come back and unfinished tasks open again.
Every crew worker is an agent with a home room, a level and XP (10 for work, 4 for a review, 3 for a test, 5 more when a task needs no loop), tools and a memory of at most 40 short entries.
Lobby, Design, Code, Review, Test, Ops and Library. While an agent works in a room its tools are cut to the room's. Ops is for the host only, and extensions can add rooms.
Tasks come from you, from Mel's plan or from agents sending work back. Idle agents bid by skill, level and machine load; every claim, hop and verdict is an event you can replay.
The owner of a machine, agent or task wins. A guest's tasks run with approval mode on, without commands or deletes, and never in Ops. Prefer the old desktop? Start with <c1/>.

Real screenshots of <c1/>, which plays a city scenario: a friend joins with six words, Dev borrows her GPU for three turns, and a task goes Design, Code, Review, Test, done. Every demo event is labeled. Not yet: Test runs the static checks (HTML, links, JS syntax, CSS, JSON), not your own test suite, and borrowing has limits per request, not a standing share.

Cloud brains, if you want them

Local by default. Add your own API key for a cloud model, per worker if you like. Keys stay in a key store on this machine; the prompts and file contents sent to that provider leave your machine, and the window says so.

Today a job that ends well is saved as a playbook, and Mel reuses it for similar requests. Next, Mel also gets a library of about 500 expert playbooks (a landing page, a form with validation, a README, a test plan and many more) and picks the closest ones for each task before the crew starts.

Today a request in the request box starts a job, and a direct message steers a worker. Next, asking for work in any chat, #general or a direct message to Dev, Designer or QA, starts real work too, with the same brief, plan, approvals and report.

What it is great at.<x1/><x2>And what it is not.</x2>
A small model on your own machine is private and free to run. It is also slower and less capable than the biggest models in a data center. Here is what to expect.
Without one, nothing is generated. The first run downloads one, 0.5 to 9.0 GB, unless a local runtime you already use is running or you add your own API key.
It is slower than it looks here
Workers take turns on one model, so a job takes minutes, not seconds. On the CPU only, the model writes a few tokens per second.
It works best with you steering
Ask for one thing at a time, read the diffs, approve the steps. Big apps in one go are out of reach for a small model.
A 0.5B or 1.5B coding model, or 3B with 16 GB of RAM
Small, single file tasks. Expect to wait.
A 3B coding model, fully on the GPU
Small and medium tasks, with you steering.
10 GB or more, or a key
A 14B coding model, a bigger one in a local runtime you already use, or a cloud model with your own API key
Tests for code you already have

Speed on a machine without a GPU
Anything at all without a model: no model, no output
It works best when you split the work, steer and approve. That is what the timeline and approval mode are for.

<x1>Your files stay on your machine.</x1> The network is used for the first run download, and then only for what you turn on: Lend mode and Code together (with a friend you paired with), GitHub, cloud providers with your own key, extensions from a URL, and the browser's speech recognition in voice mode. Lend mode sends only model prompts and answers: one request at a time, at most 20 per minute, prompts up to 120,000 characters, and the friend can stop at any time. There is no TURN relay built in, so two very strict networks may not connect.
Do I need an account or an API key?
No. The default is a model that runs on your own machine. Keys are optional, only to use your own API key for a cloud model; they are kept in a key store on this machine.
How big is the download, and how long does the first run take?

The model is 0.5 GB to 9.0 GB depending on your hardware, plus a few hundred MB for the runtime. At 100 Mbit/s the 3B model takes about 3 minutes and the 7B about 6. It happens once; after that a run is ready in the time it takes to load the model.
Will it run on a laptop without a GPU?
Yes, on the CPU with a small model: 3B with 16 GB of RAM, 1.5B with 8 to 16 GB, 0.5B below that. It is slow, a few tokens per second. Small tasks work; expect to wait.
What does the prompt refiner change?

Before planning, Mel turns your request into a brief: the goal, what to build, the constraints, the checks and any open questions. The job waits until you use the brief, edit it or keep your original. You can turn it off in Settings.
Does voice mode send my audio anywhere?

Voice uses the browser's speech recognition, which may send audio to the browser maker's service. Mel's spoken replies are made on your computer when a local voice exists. A fully local recognizer is not shipped yet.
Can a worker break my computer?

Workers only have tools scoped to the workspace folder, and paths that try to escape it are refused. Commands run with a timeout, an output cap and no network by default, and approval mode makes risky steps wait for you. Extensions run in a sandbox with the permissions you accept.
Why do the launchers trigger a security warning?
They are plain scripts that are not code signed, so Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper ask before the first run. Each one only checks for Node.js and runs <c1/>.
Can I look around without downloading a model?
Yes: <c1/> replays a scripted job. Everything it shows is labeled as a demo.
Delete <c1/> (the runtime, the models, your settings) and the <c2/> folder in your project. If you installed it with npm, also run <c3/>.

hivedesk is a free multi agent workspace: a crew of AI agents that plans and builds real files on your own computer with open source models. Invite a friend peer to peer and share a GPU. No account, no API key.
